Causes of the American Revolution
💰
Taxation Without Representation
Britain taxed colonists for things like tea and paper, but colonists had NO vote in British Parliament.
⚔️
French & Indian War Debt
Britain needed money after the war and taxed the colonies to pay for it.
📜
Intolerable Acts (1774)
Harsh British laws punishing the colonies — especially Massachusetts — after the Boston Tea Party.
🏛️
Did You Know?
"No Taxation Without Representation!"
This rallying cry united colonists against British rule. They were angry about paying taxes with NO say in government.
🤔  Check for Understanding: Name TWO reasons colonists wanted independence from Britain. VOCABULARY
Key Vocabulary
Colony
A territory settled and controlled by a faraway country.
Revolution
A sudden, complete change in government or society.
Independence
Freedom from control by another country or group.
Patriot
A colonist who wanted freedom from British rule.
Loyalist
A colonist who remained loyal to the British king.
Delegate
A person chosen to represent others and make decisions for them. FOUNDING DOCUMENTS
The Declaration of Independence
📜  What Is It?
The Declaration of Independence was signed on July 4, 1776. It told Britain — and the world — that the 13 American colonies were FREE and independent states.
Key Ideas:
All people are created equal
People have rights that cannot be taken away: Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness
Government gets its power from the people
If a government is unfair, people have the right to change it
📅  Quick Facts
Written by:
Thomas Jefferson
Signed:
July 4, 1776
Signers:
56 colonial delegates
Main idea:
Freedom from Britain
🤔  Check for Understanding: What THREE rights does the Declaration say all people have? THE REVOLUTION
The Revolutionary War
Revolutionary War Timeline (1775–1783)
1775
Battles of Lexington & Concord — 'Shot Heard Round the World'
1776
Declaration of Independence signed July 4th
1777
Battle of Saratoga — turning point, France joins colonists
1781
Battle of Yorktown — British General Cornwallis surrenders
1783
Treaty of Paris — Britain officially recognizes U.S. independence
⭐  Key People of the Revolution
George Washington — Commander of the Continental Army     Benjamin Franklin — Diplomat who won French support     King George III — British ruler the colonists fought against
🤔  Check for Understanding: What event in 1783 officially ended the Revolutionary War? VOCABULARY
More Key Vocabulary
Constitution
The written plan of government that lists the rules and laws for a country.
Amendment
A change or addition made to the Constitution.
Legislature
The branch of government that makes laws (Congress).
Democracy
A system where citizens vote and have a say in their government.
Federalism
Sharing power between the national government and state governments.
Bill of Rights
The first 10 amendments to the Constitution; protects citizens' freedoms. THE CONSTITUTION
From Articles to the Constitution
❌  Articles of Confederation (1781)
America's FIRST plan of government — but it had BIG problems:
Congress could NOT collect taxes
Congress could NOT make states obey laws
No president or national courts
Each state acted like its own country
Too weak to handle crises like Shays' Rebellion
➡️
REPLACED
by
✅  The U.S. Constitution (1787)
Written at the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia — a STRONGER plan:
Created 3 branches of government
Congress can collect taxes
Created the President (Executive Branch)
Created the Supreme Court
Included a system of checks & balances
🤔  Check for Understanding: Why did the Articles of Confederation need to be replaced? THE CONSTITUTION
Three Branches of Government
The Constitution created 3 branches so NO single person or group has too much power — this is called Checks & Balances.
🏛️  Legislative Branch
(Congress)
Makes the laws
Two parts: Senate & House of Representatives
535 members total
Can override a presidential veto
🦅  Executive Branch
(President)
Carries out the laws
Led by the President & Vice President
Commands the military
Can veto (reject) laws
⚖️  Judicial Branch
(Supreme Court)
Explains the laws
The Supreme Court has 9 justices
Can strike down unfair laws
Judges serve for life
🤔  Check for Understanding: Which branch of government makes the laws? Which branch carries out the laws? FOUNDING DOCUMENTS
The Bill of Rights
📜  The Bill of Rights = the FIRST 10 Amendments to the Constitution, added in 1791 to protect the rights of ALL citizens.
1st
Freedom of speech, religion, press, assembly, and petition
2nd
Right to keep and bear arms (weapons)
4th
Protection from unfair searches of your home
5th
You cannot be forced to testify against yourself in court
6th
Right to a speedy and fair trial by jury
8th
Protection from cruel and unusual punishment
💡  Why was the Bill of Rights added? Many Americans feared a strong central government — these amendments guaranteed personal freedoms! FIRST LEADERS
America's First Leaders
🎖️  George Washington
1st President (1789–1797)
Commander of the Continental Army during the Revolution
Presided over the Constitutional Convention
Set many traditions still followed today
Warned against political parties dividing the nation
✍️  Thomas Jefferson
3rd President / Author of the Declaration
Primary author of the Declaration of Independence
Believed strongly in individual freedoms
Purchased the Louisiana Territory, doubling U.S. size
Founded the University of Virginia
🔑  Benjamin Franklin
Founding Father / Diplomat
Helped write the Declaration of Independence
Negotiated the alliance with France during the war
Famous inventor (lightning rod, bifocals)
Helped negotiate the Treaty of Paris (1783)
🤔  Check for Understanding: What is ONE important thing George Washington did for the United States? Let's Review!
Big Ideas: A New Nation
⚔️  Revolution
Colonists fought for freedom from British taxation and unfair rule.
📜  Declaration (1776)
Declared independence; stated all people have equal rights.
🏛️  The Constitution
Created a strong national government with 3 branches & checks/balances.
⚖️  3 Branches
Legislative (laws), Executive (President), Judicial (courts).
🔟  Bill of Rights
First 10 amendments protecting citizens' freedoms (added 1791).
